threads.thread_goal: Align on current process, main gaps, and project scope before design work starts.

messages.text:
Kicking off the Cross-Department Protocol for High-Risk Detainee Health Monitoring project.

Goal for this thread: get a shared view of how health monitoring and escalation currently work on the floor, confirm the baseline process map, and agree the exact scope before we start redesigning.

I have pulled together a first draft of the current process map based on notes from intake, routine checks, and incident handling and logged it under A1, linked to T1.

Can you all share:
- How you currently spot and record health concerns during intake and patrols
- Where information tends to get lost between officers, admin, and medical
- Any units or detainee groups where the situation is different enough that we should treat them separately in scope

Once we have that, we can lock in what A1 covers and which units and detainee types this protocol will apply to.

From the custody side:
- Intake: we do a quick visual check and ask a few standard questions, but it is not written down consistently unless something is clearly wrong.
- Patrols: officers note issues in the unit log, but health notes are mixed with security events, so they are hard to track over time.
- Escalation: if someone looks unwell or behaves oddly, we call medical or the duty manager, but there is no standard threshold.

Information gaps:
- Night shift to day shift handover is patchy.
- When detainees move units, their health history does not always follow.

On scope: I suggest we start with one closed unit and the intake area, focusing on detainees flagged as vulnerable or with known medical or mental health issues. That is where the risk feels highest.

Thanks for setting this up.

From the admin desk:
- We receive paper notes and unit logs, but health-related comments are often brief, like 'not well' or 'seen by nurse', without dates or follow-up.
- When we file incident reports, health aspects are sometimes missing unless there was use of force.

For A1 and T1, I want to be sure we capture:
- Where forms are created (intake, unit, medical)
- Who actually files them and when
- How we currently index anything related to health.

On scope, I am not sure if we include segregation or just the standard closed unit and intake. Segregation has different routines. Maybe we phase that later?

From a health risk perspective, the most critical points are:
- First contact at intake
- First 24 hours in custody
- Any change in behaviour, consciousness, or breathing pattern during stay.

For A1, could we mark these as explicit checkpoints in the map? That will help later when we define indicators in A2.

On scope, I support starting with:
- Intake area
- One closed unit
- Detainees with known conditions or any vulnerability flag.

We can still observe what happens in segregation during the pilot but maybe not redesign that flow in the first round.

On the forms side, I see different layouts coming in from units, some handwritten notes on the back of other forms.

For T1 and A1, do we want to treat all those as separate steps, or just say 'officer writes note' and 'admin files note'? I am asking because later, for the checklists, it might be easier if we know how many different pieces of paper officers already handle.

Also, should we already think about where the future checklist A3 will sit in the process map, or is that for the next thread?

Good question. For A1 and T1, I suggest we:
- Show the main steps (officer records, admin files, medical updates) as separate boxes.
- Note the variety of actual paper formats in a side note, not as separate steps.

For A3, we just mark a placeholder in A1 where a standard checklist would be used at intake and during patrols. The detailed design can stay in the later thread.

I will update A1 accordingly and share a short summary once done.

On segregation: routines are stricter, and we already have extra observation there. If we mix that into the first version, we might overcomplicate things.

I would keep segregation out of the initial protocol scope but still log any health incidents from there so we can see if the new approach should be extended later.

For detainee types, I would include:
- All new arrivals in intake
- In the pilot unit, anyone with a vulnerability or medical flag, plus anyone involved in a recent incident.

Understood. So for scope we are leaning towards:
- Locations: intake area and one closed unit
- Detainees: new arrivals plus those with vulnerability or medical flags in that unit
- Excluding segregation from the first design, but still monitoring incidents there.

If everyone agrees, I will reflect that in T1 and in the description of A1 as the baseline.

That scope works for the health content as well. It covers the riskiest phases without stretching the pilot too wide.

One small addition for A1: can we mark where medical staff currently enter the picture, even if it is informal? For example, direct calls from officers versus referrals through admin. That will matter later when we define escalation in A5.

Yes, I can add two separate steps in A1 for:
- Officer calls medical directly
- Officer reports to admin or manager, who then contacts medical.

I will also note where there is no written trace today. That should help when we design the central log A4 later.

I will circulate the updated A1 by end of day and ask for a quick check that it matches reality on the floor.

Once you share A1, I will walk through it against a typical shift in the closed unit and flag anything missing.

One thing to check: night shift often uses a different notebook for quick notes before they are copied into the main log. If that is not in A1, we should add it as a step where information can get lost.

Good point on the night notebook. I will check with the admin team how those notes are currently filed, if at all, and we can add that to T1 as a known gap.

Once A1 is updated, I suggest we treat it as our working baseline for the design work, unless someone spots a major error.

I have now updated A1 with:
- Intake and first 24 hours checkpoints
- Separate paths for direct medical calls and referrals
- Night shift notebook as a distinct step with a risk note.

Unless there are objections by tomorrow noon, I propose we confirm A1 as the baseline current-state map for this project and move on to defining indicators in the next thread.

I have reviewed the updated A1 against our shift routine in the closed unit. It matches what we actually do, including the informal bits.

From my side, we can treat A1 as the baseline. If we discover small variations later, we can note them, but they should not block the design.

Given the agreement here, I will record that:
- Scope is intake plus one closed unit, focusing on new arrivals and detainees with vulnerability or medical flags, excluding segregation from the first design.
- A1 is our confirmed current-state baseline for T1 and for the rest of the project.

I will note this in the project summary so we can reference it later when we discuss the SOP and pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Define practical health risk indicators and observation checklists for officers.

messages.text:
Picking up on indicators and checklists.

I have drafted a list of health risk indicators for officers, linked to T2 and captured in a working version of A2. They are grouped into:
- Breathing and consciousness
- Visible injuries and pain
- Behaviour and mood changes
- Self-harm and suicide warning signs
- Substance use and withdrawal signs.

I also sketched how these could appear in a short observation checklist for intake and patrols, which would become A3 under T4.

From your side, I need to know:
- Which items are realistic to observe quickly during intake and on patrol
- Where wording feels too technical
- How many lines you can reasonably fill in without slowing down your shift.

Once we refine the list, we can lock the final indicators for A2 and agree the structure and length of A3.

From the unit perspective:
- Intake: we can spend a bit more time, but it still needs to be under a few minutes per person.
- Patrols: we have seconds at each door, so anything that requires long observation will not work.

The groups you listed make sense. For patrols, I would focus on:
- Consciousness (responsive, confused, not responding)
- Breathing (normal, laboured, very fast, very slow)
- Obvious injuries or bleeding
- Clear distress or agitation.

For self-harm and withdrawal, we can note obvious signs, but subtle ones might be hard to spot on a quick round. Maybe those are better as prompts for when we already have a concern.

On the checklist layout for A3 and T4, I was thinking of:
- One page for intake
- One page for patrols, maybe half a page if we can.

Would it work if we use simple tick boxes like 'OK' or 'Concern' next to each group, and a small space for notes? That might be faster than writing full sentences.

I am not sure how many lines we should plan for per detainee on the patrol sheet. Maybe officers can advise what is realistic.

From an admin and filing angle, it would help if:
- Intake checklist A3 clearly identifies the detainee and date so we can file it with the intake pack.
- Patrol observations can be summarised into the central log A4 later without rewriting everything.

For T2 and T4, could we:
- Limit the number of indicators per group to the most critical ones
- Use plain words like 'very sleepy' instead of medical terms.

That should also make it easier to train staff later under T6.

Thanks, that helps narrow things down.

Proposal for A2:
- For intake: keep all five groups but limit each to 3 to 4 key indicators.
- For patrols: focus on a shorter subset, mainly consciousness, breathing, obvious injury, and visible distress, plus a single line for 'other serious concern'.

For wording, I will avoid medical jargon. For example, instead of 'respiratory distress', we can say 'breathing very hard or very fast'.

If that sounds workable, I will adjust the draft A2 and share a short example of how it would look on A3.

That structure works for us.

On the patrol sheet A3, I would suggest:
- One line per detainee per round is too much; maybe we only record when there is a concern.
- So the checklist could be 'only fill when you see a problem', with tick boxes for which group triggered it.

For intake, we can fill the full list because we are already sitting with the person.

If we only fill the patrol checklist when there is a concern, I can design A3 so that:
- The top has detainee and date fields.
- Below, there are repeated blocks with tick boxes for the indicator groups and a small notes area.

For T4, I will mock up a version with space for, say, 6 concern entries per sheet. If that is not enough, officers can use a second sheet.

Does that sound manageable on a busy shift?

On the wording, I have gone through the draft A2 and replaced technical terms with plain phrases, for example:
- 'Very drowsy, hard to wake up'
- 'Says chest hurts or cannot catch breath'
- 'Talking about wanting to die or hurt themselves'.

I will keep the total number of indicators to around 15 to 18 across all groups, with a clear note that officers are not diagnosing, just observing.

Once we agree on this list, we can treat it as final for A2 and use it as the reference for training under T6.

From a documentation side, having a fixed list of around 15 to 18 indicators in A2 is fine. It is short enough to fit into training and into the SOP A5 later.

For A3 and T4, I suggest we:
- Use the same group headings as in A2 so officers do not have to learn two different structures.
- Add a simple 'action taken' tick box (for example, informed medical, informed supervisor) so that later we can transfer that into the central log A4.

If everyone is comfortable with the current indicator list, we can mark A2 as agreed and focus on finalising the checklist layout.

I have read through the latest A2 draft. The phrases are clear and match what we actually see on the landings.

From the officer side, I am fine treating this list as the reference for when we should escalate. We can always add rare edge cases in training, but the core list looks right.

So I am ok to say the indicator list in A2 is agreed.

I will update the A3 layout under T4 to:
- Use the same group headings as A2
- Include tick boxes for 'informed medical' and 'informed supervisor'
- Keep intake on one page and patrol concerns as repeated blocks.

To keep it short, I will aim for:
- Intake: no more than 20 tick boxes total
- Patrol: 6 concern entries per sheet.

If that works, we can treat this structure and length as final for A3.

That sounds workable. Intake on one page is fine, and 6 concern entries per patrol sheet should cover a typical round. If we have more than that, it is probably a serious situation anyway.

From my side, we can go ahead with that structure and length for A3.

Great, I will:
- Freeze the agreed indicator list in A2 for T2
- Align the wording in A3 with A2 so officers see the same phrases in both.

This will also feed directly into the training materials under T6, where we can walk through a few examples using the checklist.

threads.thread_goal: Lock down the SOP, logging template, and filing workflow.

messages.text:
Moving on to the SOP and logging.

I have drafted:
- A health risk assessment and escalation SOP, captured in A5 and linked to T3
- A central health monitoring log template A4 with a basic filing workflow under T5.

The SOP A5 covers:
- Who is responsible for initial observation, escalation, and documentation
- When to escalate based on the indicators in A2
- How to record actions in A3 and transfer them into A4.

The log A4 is a simple table that can be printed and filed daily.

I need your input on:
- Whether the escalation steps and responsibilities are realistic on the floor
- Whether the log format and storage routine fit with current correctional procedures and admin capacity.

Once we refine these, we also need to document alignment with existing rules in A8 under T11.

On the SOP A5:
- The basic flow (officer observes, uses A3, informs supervisor or medical, records in A4) makes sense.
- One concern: in urgent cases, we go straight to emergency response and medical, then document later. The SOP should be clear that nothing delays that.

On responsibilities:
- It is fine that officers start the record, but we need clarity on who ensures A4 is updated and filed each day. I would suggest the unit supervisor signs off the daily A4 sheet.

On A4 format, the columns look ok, but we should keep the number of fields per entry low so it does not become another long form.

From the admin side, for T5 and T11:
- We can store A4 sheets in a central binder per unit, with a daily index at the front.
- At the end of each week, admin can archive the binder pages in the health monitoring file.

For A8, I will need to map the SOP steps in A5 to existing correctional procedures and legal use-of-force rules. I will draft a short memo and then ask management or compliance to review it.

On A4 fields, I suggest we keep to: detainee ID, date and time, indicator group, short description, action taken, and initials of the person recording.

On the escalation thresholds in A5, I have aligned them with the indicators in A2:
- Any serious breathing problem, chest pain, or loss of consciousness triggers immediate medical contact and emergency response.
- Clear self-harm intent or attempt triggers immediate escalation to supervisor and medical.
- Moderate concerns (for example, mild confusion, visible but not severe injury) trigger same-day medical review.

The SOP text makes it clear that emergency response always comes before paperwork.

If you see any conflict with current correctional procedures, we should adjust the wording before we finalise A5 and A8.

Looking at A4 from a layout point of view for T5:
- I can format it so that each line is one observation, with clear columns and enough space for handwriting.
- We can add a small box at the bottom for the supervisor to sign off the day.

For filing, I will make sure the footer has unit, date, and page number so admin can keep pages in order even if they get separated.

I have updated A5 so that:
- The first step in any severe case is clearly 'call emergency and medical immediately'.
- Documentation in A3 and A4 happens as soon as the situation is under control, not before.

On responsibilities, I have added that:
- Officers complete A3 and initial entries in A4.
- Unit supervisors review and sign A4 daily.
- Admin staff file A4 and maintain the weekly archive.

Please check if this matches how roles are usually assigned on the floor.

The updated A5 reads well and matches how we handle emergencies now, just with clearer steps.

The division of tasks between officers, supervisors, and admin is also in line with current practice. The only thing I would add is that if the supervisor is not on site, the duty manager can sign A4.

With that small tweak, I am comfortable with the escalation steps and responsibilities as written.

I have started the compliance memo A8 under T11 and mapped the main SOP steps in A5 to:
- Existing health and safety procedures
- Incident reporting rules
- Legal use-of-force guidance.

I do not see any direct conflicts, but I will send A8 to a compliance representative and prison management for review before we call it final.

On A4, I agree with the fields we listed. Keeping it to one line per observation should help with auditability without adding too much work.

I have added the duty manager as an alternative signatory for A4 in A5 and in the T5 description.

To confirm, the escalation chain in A5 now reads:
- Officer observes and records using A3
- For serious concerns, officer calls emergency and medical immediately
- Officer informs supervisor or duty manager
- Supervisor or duty manager ensures A4 is updated and signs off daily.

If there are no further changes, we can treat the escalation steps and responsibilities in A5 as agreed.

I have rechecked the latest A5. The chain you described matches what we can do operationally.

From the officer side, I am fine signing off on these escalation steps and responsibilities.

I have updated the A4 layout for T5 with:
- One line per observation
- Clear columns for the fields we agreed
- A signature box for supervisor or duty manager.

For the filing routine, I added a small note at the top of A4 reminding staff to place completed sheets in the unit binder at the end of each shift.

I have tested the updated A4 with some sample data for T5. It fits on one page per day for a typical unit, and the binder routine is workable for admin.

Assuming compliance signs off on A8, I think we can confirm both the format of A4 and the storage routine as our standard approach.

Compliance has now reviewed A8 and confirmed that A5 and A4 align with existing procedures, with no changes requested.

Given that, I propose we:
- Confirm the final format and daily filing routine for A4 as described in T5
- Treat A8 as the reference for any future audits.

If there are no objections, we can record this as agreed and move on to pilot planning in the next thread.

From the unit side, the A4 format and filing routine you described are workable. The daily sign-off is a good discipline and should not add much time.

I am fine confirming this as our standard log format and storage routine.

Noted. I will update the project summary so that:
- A5 is the agreed escalation SOP under T3
- A4 and its filing routine under T5 are confirmed
- A8 under T11 documents the alignment with correctional procedures.

This gives us a solid base to plan the pilot in the next thread.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and execute the pilot, then consolidate feedback and improvements.

messages.text:
Time to plan the pilot.

Based on our earlier scope, I have drafted a pilot plan in A6 under T7. The proposal is to:
- Run the pilot in one closed unit plus the intake area
- Use the agreed A2 indicators, A3 checklists, A4 log, and A5 SOP
- Run it for one full rota cycle so we cover all shifts.

We need to agree on:
- Which specific unit will be the pilot site
- Exact start and end dates
- Which officers and admin staff will participate.

After the pilot, we will capture feedback in A7 under T8, refine forms under T9, update SOP and training under T10, and then prepare the final summary and rollout recommendation under T12.

For the pilot unit, I suggest we use the B-wing closed unit:
- It has a mix of detainees, including some with health and vulnerability flags.
- The team there is used to trying new procedures.

On timing, starting next Monday and running for one full rota cycle (three weeks) would give us enough coverage.

Participating staff:
- All officers on B-wing shifts
- Intake officers during the same period
- The unit supervisor and duty managers for sign-off on A4.

We should check with prison management to confirm they are comfortable with B-wing as the pilot site.

From the admin side for T7 and T8:
- We can support B-wing and intake with filing A4 and collecting A3 forms.
- I can draft the briefing invites and share A6 with prison management for approval.

For A6, I will add:
- The proposed dates (next Monday to three weeks later)
- The list of participating roles (officers, supervisors, admin).

Once management confirms, we can schedule short training sessions under T6 and send out the invites.

For the pilot, I will:
- Run short briefings for B-wing and intake staff under T6, using A2, A3, A4, and A5 as the core materials.
- Include 2 to 3 quick scenarios so officers can practice using the checklist and deciding when to escalate.

For A7 under T8, I suggest we collect feedback on:
- How easy it was to use A3 and A4
- Whether the SOP A5 fit real incidents
- Any confusion around the indicators in A2.

We can then use that to refine layouts under T9 and update SOP and training under T10.

For T9, during the pilot I will ask officers to mark on A3 and A4 where the layout is awkward or there is not enough space.

After we collect feedback in A7, I can:
- Adjust font size and spacing on A3 and A4
- Maybe add small icons next to the indicator groups to make them easier to scan quickly.

I will wait for the first week of pilot feedback before making any changes, so we do not confuse staff mid-way.

B-wing plus intake sounds like a good pilot scope. I have updated A6 under T7 with:
- Pilot site: B-wing closed unit and intake area
- Duration: next Monday for three weeks
- Participating staff: B-wing officers, intake officers, supervisors, duty managers, and admin.

I will send A6 to prison management today for confirmation. Assuming they agree, we can treat this as the final pilot setup.

Once management signs off on A6, I will brief the B-wing team informally so they know what is coming, and we can line up any questions for the formal training.

During the pilot under T8, I will:
- Make sure A3 and A4 are actually used on shifts
- Collect feedback from at least three officers and two assistants for A7.

We should also note any incidents where the protocol was not followed, so we can understand why.

Prison management has now reviewed A6 and agreed to the B-wing and intake pilot with the proposed dates.

I will:
- Send calendar invites for the briefings under T6
- Share A6, A2, A3, A4, and A5 with the participating staff.

With that, we can consider the pilot unit, dates, and participating staff confirmed as per A6.

I will run two short briefing sessions under T6 before the pilot starts:
- One for B-wing officers and supervisors
- One for intake staff.

Each session will:
- Walk through A2 indicators and A5 SOP
- Practice filling A3 and A4 using simple scenarios
- Clarify what to do in emergencies versus routine concerns.

I will also explain how we will collect feedback for A7 so staff know their input will shape the final version.

Pilot update after week one:
- Officers are using A3 at intake consistently; on patrols, they mostly fill it when there is a clear concern, as planned.
- A4 is being completed daily, but some entries are missing the 'action taken' field.

Feedback so far for A7:
- A3 intake page is clear, but a few officers asked for a 'medication mentioned' tick box.
- On A4, the lines are a bit tight when writing longer notes.

No major issues with A5; in emergencies, staff still prioritised response over paperwork, which is correct.

Based on that feedback for T9:
- I can add a small 'medication mentioned' tick box to the intake A3 page.
- I will slightly increase the line height on A4 to give more space for notes.

I will prepare updated drafts of A3 and A4 but only roll them out after the pilot ends, so we do not change forms mid-way. We can still test the new layout with a couple of officers before finalising.

Thanks for the week-one update. For A7 under T8, I will start drafting the evaluation report with sections on:
- Usability of A3 and A4
- How well A5 worked in real incidents
- Any training gaps from T6.

Please keep noting specific examples where fields were left blank or where the SOP was hard to follow. Concrete cases will help us decide which changes to adopt before rollout.

End-of-pilot summary from the floor for A7:
- A3: Officers like the structure. The main asks are the 'medication mentioned' tick box and slightly clearer wording on one of the behaviour items.
- A4: Works, but we definitely need a bit more space per line. The daily sign-off is happening.
- A5: The escalation steps are clear. The only confusion was around who calls medical in borderline cases; we clarified that the officer can call directly.

Overall, staff are positive and would keep using the protocol if the small layout tweaks are made.

From the training and health angle, the pilot showed that:
- Staff understood the indicators in A2 and used them consistently.
- The main issues were practical (space on forms, one or two phrases needing simplification), not with the core content.

For T10, I will update the training materials to:
- Include the 'medication mentioned' example
- Clarify that officers can call medical directly in borderline cases, as already reflected in A5.

I would recommend we adopt the layout changes proposed under T9 before wider rollout.

I have now applied the pilot feedback in A7 to the forms under T9:
- Added 'medication mentioned' tick box to A3 intake
- Increased line spacing on A4
- Slightly simplified one behaviour phrase to match how officers talk.

These are the only layout changes I propose before rollout. Anything more complex might require reprinting too often.

In the draft evaluation report A7 under T8, I have summarised the recommended changes before rollout as:
- Accept the A3 and A4 layout tweaks from T9
- Clarify in A5 and training that officers can call medical directly in borderline cases
- Emphasise in training that 'action taken' on A4 should always be filled.

Unless there are objections, I suggest we adopt exactly these changes before recommending wider rollout in T12.

From the officer side, those three changes match what we asked for and are enough to make the protocol workable day to day.

I do not see a need for any additional changes before rollout. I am comfortable adopting these as the final adjustments based on the pilot feedback in A7.

Noted. I will:
- Finalise A7 with those agreed changes
- Update A5 and the training materials under T10 accordingly
- Prepare the final project summary and rollout recommendation under T12, proposing that we extend the protocol to other similar units after a short bedding-in period on B-wing.

This will close out the pilot phase and set us up for wider implementation.
